front: This lesson names three main categories of distribution. What are they?
answer: Online distribution / Physical platforms / Physical media
title: Distribution Platforms

front: This lesson names four types of physical platform. What are they?
answer: Computers / Interactive TV / Kiosks / Mobile devices
title: Distribution Platforms

front: Why can a video made for a Blu-ray disc use a less compressed, higher quality format than one for website streaming?
answer: The disc has far more storage capacity and the player can handle larger files.
title: Distribution Platforms

front: Why does physical media cost more to distribute than online distribution?
answer: It must be manufactured and physically delivered, adding manufacturing, printing and postage costs.
title: Distribution Platforms

front: This lesson's comparison table lists five bitmap image formats. What are they?
answer: JPEG / PNG / GIF / TIFF / BMP
title: Image File Properties and Compression

front: This lesson's comparison table lists three vector image formats. What are they?
answer: SVG / PDF / EPS
title: Image File Properties and Compression

front: Why does a JPEG lose a little quality every time it is edited and re-saved?
answer: Its lossy compression permanently removes a little image data each time the file is saved.
title: Image File Properties and Compression

front: Why is a RAW file usually converted to another format before it is distributed?
answer: It contains maximum unprocessed image data, so it must be exported to a smaller format like JPEG first.
title: Image File Properties and Compression

front: This lesson names three categories of audio file format. What are they?
answer: Uncompressed / Lossless compressed / Lossy compressed
title: Audio File Properties and Formats

front: This lesson names three lossy compressed audio formats. What are they?
answer: MP3 / AAC / OGG Vorbis
title: Audio File Properties and Formats

front: Why is 44,100 Hz used as the standard sample rate for music, rather than a lower value?
answer: It must be at least double the highest frequency humans can hear, plus a small safety margin.
title: Audio File Properties and Formats

front: Why does WAV produce a much larger file than the same recording saved as MP3?
answer: WAV stores sound with no compression at all, while MP3 removes audio data most listeners cannot hear.
title: Audio File Properties and Formats

front: This lesson names five resolution standards. What are they?
answer: SD / HD / UHD / 4K / 8K
title: Moving Image File Properties

front: Why does H.265 suit 4K video better than H.264, even though it needs more powerful hardware?
answer: It gives similar quality to H.264 at about half the file size, which suits 4K's much larger data.
title: Moving Image File Properties

front: Why does a video at 60 fps produce a much larger file than the same video at 30 fps?
answer: It contains twice as many frames each second, so twice as much data must be stored.
title: Moving Image File Properties

front: Every media product goes through three phases of production named in this lesson. What are they?
answer: Pre-production / Production / Post-production
title: Work Plans and Time Management

front: Why does listing resources in advance in a work plan help keep a project's budget accurate?
answer: It makes sure equipment is booked and the right people are available at the right time.
title: Work Plans and Time Management

front: Why can a camera crew plan other work around a delay, instead of turning up to find the set isn't ready?
answer: The work plan lets them see the delay in advance, so they can schedule other work for the days before.
title: Work Plans and Time Management

front: This lesson lists six conventions of a well-constructed mind map. What are they?
answer: Central topic / Main branches / Sub-branches / Keywords / Colour coding / Images and icons
title: Mind Maps and Mood Boards

front: Why is a physical mood board harder to share with a client working remotely?
answer: It exists only as a physical object, such as printed images and swatches, so it cannot be sent online.
title: Mind Maps and Mood Boards

front: Why can't a digital mood board fully show how a fabric or material will feel?
answer: It displays only images on a screen, so real textures and materials cannot be conveyed accurately.
title: Mind Maps and Mood Boards

front: This lesson names six planning documents used in pre-production. What are they?
answer: Asset logs / Flowcharts / Scripts / Storyboards / Visualisation diagrams / Wireframe layouts
title: Asset Logs and Flowcharts

front: Why are digital flowcharts generally easier to work with than hand-drawn ones?
answer: They can be edited and shared far more easily than a hand-drawn version.
title: Asset Logs and Flowcharts

front: Why does an interactive product like a website or app need a flowchart, while simple linear content does not?
answer: A flowchart maps the choices and paths a user can take, which only interactive products have.
title: Asset Logs and Flowcharts

front: This lesson lists six formatting conventions used in a professional script. What are they?
answer: Scene heading / Action or description / Character name / Dialogue / Parenthetical / Transitions
title: Scripts and Storyboards

front: Why does a printed magazine not need a storyboard, unlike a TV advert?
answer: A storyboard plans a sequence of camera shots, and a magazine has no moving images to sequence.
title: Scripts and Storyboards

front: Why are scripts and storyboards usually used together on a professional production?
answer: The script gives the dialogue and scene details in words, while the storyboard turns these into a visual shot sequence.
title: Scripts and Storyboards

front: This lesson lists six things a good visualisation diagram includes. What are they?
answer: Layout sketch / Annotations / Colour indications / Font or typography choices / Image placeholders / Dimensions
title: Visualisation Diagrams and Wireframes

front: This lesson lists six conventions wireframes follow. What are they?
answer: Boxes and rectangles / Lines of text (lorem ipsum) / Crossed boxes / Navigation elements / No colour or styling / Labels
title: Visualisation Diagrams and Wireframes

front: Why is a visualisation diagram used for a magazine page, but a wireframe used for a website?
answer: A magazine page is a static, visual product, while a website's early planning focuses on structure, not visuals.
title: Visualisation Diagrams and Wireframes

front: Why do wireframes use a crossed box instead of a real photo to mark image space?
answer: A wireframe is deliberately plain, with no colour or real images, to keep focus on structure rather than appearance.
title: Visualisation Diagrams and Wireframes
problems: names a board or the exam

front: This lesson names six camera angles. What are they?
answer: Eye level / High angle / Low angle / Bird's eye (aerial) / Worm's eye / Dutch angle
title: Camera Shots, Angles and Movement

front: Why does a handheld camera shot suit a chase scene in an action film?
answer: Its shaky, unstabilised movement conveys urgency and realism, increasing the audience's sense of tension.
title: Camera Shots, Angles and Movement

front: Why might a director use a crane shot rising above a city at the start of a film?
answer: A rising crane shot establishes the setting and creates a sense of scale for the audience.
title: Camera Shots, Angles and Movement

front: This lesson names three main types of intellectual property relevant to media. What are they?
answer: Copyright / Trademarks / Patents
title: Legal Issues: Copyright, Trademarks and Privacy

front: This lesson names four legal options for using someone else's copyrighted work. What are they?
answer: Creative Commons licences / Fair dealing / Permissions, fees or licences / Watermarks and symbols
title: Legal Issues: Copyright, Trademarks and Privacy

front: Why can violating someone's privacy be costly for a media producer, not just upsetting for the person filmed?
answer: It can lead to legal action, fines, loss of professional reputation and even criminal prosecution for the producer.
title: Legal Issues: Copyright, Trademarks and Privacy

front: Why is it illegal to use another company's trademark in a media product without permission?
answer: It could confuse consumers about who made the product or damage the trademark owner's brand.
title: Legal Issues: Copyright, Trademarks and Privacy

front: This lesson names four regulatory bodies you must know. What are they?
answer: ASA / Ofcom / BBFC / PEGI
title: Regulation, Certification, Health and Safety

front: This lesson names six categories of health and safety risk on a media shoot. What are they?
answer: Electrical hazards / Manual handling / Working at height / Lone working / Environmental hazards / Fire risks
title: Regulation, Certification, Health and Safety

front: Why might a film aimed at teenagers lose much of its audience if it receives an 18 certificate?
answer: An 18 certificate restricts the film to adults only, cutting off the teenage viewers it was made for.
title: Regulation, Certification, Health and Safety

front: Why do cables on a film set need to be taped down?
answer: Loose cables lying around the set can trip crew members, so they are taped down.
title: Regulation, Certification, Health and Safety

front: This lesson names five purposes of media products. What are they?
answer: Advertise or promote / Educate / Entertain / Inform / Influence
title: Purpose, Style, Content and Layout

front: Why does a media product's purpose come first when choosing things like colour and font?
answer: All the style choices, such as colour and language, work together to help the product achieve its purpose.
title: Purpose, Style, Content and Layout

front: Why can a single media product have more than one purpose, such as an educational game?
answer: It can combine two purposes at once — an educational game both educates and entertains its audience.
title: Purpose, Style, Content and Layout

front: This lesson names six ways a client brief can be communicated. What are they?
answer: Commission / Formal brief / Informal brief / Meeting or discussion / Negotiated brief / Written brief
title: Client Requirements and Communication

front: Why can't a production team use dark themes or complex language for a children's charity video, even if it looks more striking?
answer: The client's brief and ethos require a family-friendly style, so those choices would break the client's requirements.
title: Client Requirements and Communication

front: Why does a negotiated brief usually take longer to agree than a formal brief?
answer: Both the client and the production team must contribute ideas and agree together, which takes extra time.
title: Client Requirements and Communication

front: This lesson lists five BBFC categories used to rate films. What are they?
title: Audience Demographics and Segmentation

front: This lesson lists five PEGI age ratings for digital games. What are they?
title: Audience Demographics and Segmentation

front: Why do classification systems like BBFC and PEGI use age ratings?
answer: They protect audiences, especially children, from content that may not be suitable for their age group.
title: Audience Demographics and Segmentation

front: Why might a product aimed at a luxury audience use gold and black colours with elegant typography?
answer: Luxury audiences expect a premium design, so producers use elegant colours and typography to match that expectation.
title: Audience Demographics and Segmentation

front: This lesson names four primary research methods. What are they?
answer: Focus groups / Interviews / Online surveys / Questionnaires
title: Research Methods: Primary and Secondary

front: This lesson names four secondary research sources. What are they?
answer: Books and journals / Internet sites or research / Magazines and newspapers / Television
title: Research Methods: Primary and Secondary

front: Why might a focus group's feedback be skewed rather than reflecting the whole group's views?
answer: Dominant voices in the group can influence how others answer, skewing the group's overall opinion.
title: Research Methods: Primary and Secondary

front: Why is quantitative data easier to present as charts and graphs than qualitative data?
answer: It is numerical, so it can be measured, counted and turned into statistics for a chart.
title: Research Methods: Primary and Secondary

front: This lesson names four transitions used between shots. What are they?
answer: Cut / Dissolve or crossfade / Fade to black / Wipe
title: Media Codes: Camera Techniques

front: This lesson names four types of camera movement. What are they?
answer: Pan / Tilt / Track / Zoom
title: Media Codes: Camera Techniques

front: Why is a medium close-up commonly used for interviews rather than an extreme close-up?
answer: It balances facial expression with body language, which suits interviews and dialogue scenes.
title: Media Codes: Camera Techniques

front: Why do horror films often use extreme close-ups and close-ups to build suspense?
answer: They show emotion and draw attention to a small detail, building tension for the audience.
title: Media Codes: Camera Techniques

front: This lesson names five types of audio code. What are they?
answer: Dialogue / Music genre / Silence / Sound effects / Vocal intonation
title: Media Codes: Mise-en-Scene

front: This lesson names six things mise-en-scene includes. What are they?
answer: Setting / Lighting / Costume / Props / Colour / Arrangement of characters
title: Media Codes: Mise-en-Scene

front: Why might a sudden silence right after a loud explosion make an audience feel the shock more strongly?
answer: Silence can feel more powerful than any sound, so a sudden silence after an explosion makes the shock hit harder.
title: Media Codes: Mise-en-Scene

front: Why does a red rose in an advert connote love or passion, even though it is literally just a flower?
answer: Its denotation is just a flower, but its connotation is the symbolic meaning of love or passion it suggests.
title: Media Codes: Mise-en-Scene

front: This course covers four topic areas. What are they?
answer: The media industry / Factors influencing product design / Pre-production planning / Distribution considerations
title: Introduction to Creative iMedia

front: This lesson names five words used to signal what a written answer should include. What are they?
answer: Identify / Describe / Explain / Discuss / Outline
title: Introduction to Creative iMedia

front: This lesson names four traditional media sectors. What are they?
answer: Film / Television / Radio / Print publishing
title: Sectors of the Media Industry

front: This lesson names four new media sectors. What are they?
answer: Computer games / Interactive media / Internet / Digital publishing
title: Sectors of the Media Industry

front: Why can a new media channel react to changes far faster than a scheduled TV broadcast?
answer: New media channels can be updated minute by minute, while traditional channels take much longer to produce content.
title: Sectors of the Media Industry

front: Why does convergence mean a newspaper is no longer only a traditional media product?
answer: It merges a traditional print edition with a website carrying video content, which counts as new media.
title: Sectors of the Media Industry

front: This lesson names five types of animation. What are they?
answer: Traditional or cel animation / 2D animation / 3D animation / Motion graphics / Stop motion
title: Products in the Media Industry

front: Why is a fully immersive VR headset different from an AR app like a phone camera filter?
answer: VR fully replaces the user's real world with a simulated one, while AR only overlays digital images onto it.
title: Products in the Media Industry

front: Why does stop motion animation only show movement once the photographs are played back in sequence?
answer: Physical objects are moved slightly between each photograph, and playing the photos in sequence creates the illusion of movement.
title: Products in the Media Industry

front: This lesson names three categories of job role in the media industry. What are they?
answer: Creative roles / Technical roles / Senior roles
title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 1)

front: This lesson names three production phases a media project goes through. What are they?
answer: Pre-production / Production / Post-production
title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 1)

front: Why does a script writer's work have to be finished before filming can start?
answer: Script writers work only in pre-production, and their script must be finished before filming begins.
title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 1)

front: Why does an animator's work span all three production phases, unlike a photographer's?
answer: An animator researches, creates and refines the animation across all three phases, while a photographer mainly shoots during production.
title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 1)

front: This lesson names five senior roles in the media industry. What are they?
answer: Campaign manager / Creative director / Director / Editor / Production manager
title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 2)

front: This lesson names five transferable skills developed by this course. What are they?
answer: Creative thinking / Analytical skills / Digital presentation / Planning / Problem solving
title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 2)

front: Why might a small media project use just one person for several jobs, instead of separate specialists?
answer: A small project's limited size and scale means it does not need a separate specialist for every single role.
title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 2)

front: Why does a production manager's job differ from a director's, even though both work across every phase of a project?
answer: A production manager handles the practical logistics, while a director makes the creative and artistic decisions.
title: Job Roles in the Media Industry (Part 2)
